original_value:
We propose a real-time method for the infrastructure-free estimation of articulated human motion. The approach leverages a swarm of camera-equipped flying robots and
            jointly
            optimizes the swarm's and skeletal states, which include the 3D joint positions and a set of bones. Our method allows to track the motion of human subjects, for example an athlete, over long time horizons and long distances, in challenging settings and at large scale, where fixed infrastructure approaches are not applicable. The proposed algorithm uses active infra-red markers, runs in real-time and accurately estimates robot and human pose parameters online without the need for accurately calibrated or stationary mounted cameras. Our method i) estimates a global coordinate frame for the MAV swarm, ii) jointly optimizes the human pose and relative camera positions, and iii) estimates the length of the human bones. The entire swarm is then controlled via a model predictive controller to maximize visibility of the subject from multiple viewpoints even under fast motion such as jumping or jogging. We demonstrate our method in a number of difficult scenarios including capture of long locomotion sequences at the scale of a triplex gym, in non-planar terrain, while climbing and in outdoor scenarios.

result.paraphrase: We propose a real-time, infrastructure-free method for estimating articulated human motion. It uses a swarm of camera-equipped flying robots and jointly optimizes the swarm state together with skeletal state, including 3D joint positions and a set of bones. The method can track human subjects, such as an athlete, over long distances and long time horizons in challenging, large-scale settings where fixed infrastructure approaches are not suitable. Using active infra-red markers, the algorithm runs in real time and accurately estimates robot and human pose parameters online without requiring accurately calibrated or stationary mounted cameras. Specifically, it i) estimates a global coordinate frame for the MAV swarm, ii) jointly optimizes human pose and relative camera positions, and iii) estimates human bone lengths. A model predictive controller then coordinates the entire swarm to maximize multi-view visibility of the subject, even during fast motion such as jumping or jogging. We demonstrate the method in difficult scenarios, including long locomotion sequences across the scale of a triplex gym, on non-planar terrain, while climbing, and outdoors.
